lesson.menu_title: Advanced Speaking -- Thinking on Your Feet: Answering Without Preparation
lesson.menu_desc: At the leadership offsite, the questions come with no warning. Read a method for impromptu answers, buy time without sounding lost, and say how sure you are with modals of deduction -- "It must be the old data again", "She might ask about the cost", "That can't be right"
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 26 -- Advanced Speaking -- Thinking on Your Feet: Answering Without Preparation
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Carlos Vinicius Vale Bassan | Lesson 26 -- Thinking on Your Feet
lesson.grammar_point: modals of deduction (must, might, could, can't + be / have + past participle)

listenings.text: When someone asks you a question you did not prepare for, your brain wants to do two things: panic, or talk too much. Here is a better plan. First, buy time honestly. Say: that is a good question, let me think for a second. Three seconds of silence sound confident, not lost. Second, tell people how sure you are. If you are almost certain, use must: it must be the old data. If you are not sure, use might or could: it might be the timing. And if something is impossible, use can't: that can't be right, we checked it twice. Third, make one point, give one reason, and stop. Rambling is the real enemy. Nobody remembers your fifth sentence, but everybody remembers if you had a clear first one.

Hi Carlos, Mark Ellison here. Just a quick heads-up for tomorrow's leadership offsite. Our new CFO will be in the room. She must have read the post-mortem, because she asked me about it this morning. She might ask you about the final cost of the bridge, and she could ask about the next integration, too. Do not worry about exact numbers. A ballpark figure is fine, and if you do not know, an educated guess is better than silence. One more thing: the session starts at nine and there are twelve people on the list, so the questions will come fast. Keep your answers short. See you tomorrow.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
words: Off the top of my head
defs: to talk for too long without a clear point
a number that is approximately right, not exact
without checking or thinking for long
quickly, while something is already happening
a strong feeling that you cannot fully explain
a guess based on some knowledge or experience
to get a few more seconds or minutes before you answer

reading.rtitle: How to Think on Your Feet
paras: In a senior role, the hardest questions often come without warning: in the elevator, at the end of a meeting, or in an open Q&A with the whole leadership team. You cannot prepare for every impromptu question. What you can prepare is a method. People who answer well on the fly are not smarter than everyone else; they simply have a routine.

The first step is to buy time without sounding lost. A short phrase like “Let me think about that for a second” gives you three or four seconds, and it sounds calm. The second step is to say how sure you are. If you do not have the data, you can still give a ballpark figure or an educated guess, as long as you make it clear that it is an estimate: “Off the top of my head, it might be around ten percent.” Senior people respect that honesty much more than an invented number.

The last step is to stop. The biggest risk is not a wrong answer; it is to ramble. When we are nervous, we keep talking to fill the silence, and the main point disappears. Make one point, give one reason, add one example, and stop. If your gut feeling is strong, say it, and then offer to confirm the numbers later.
